It is, of course, permissible for an hon. member to point out the inadequacies of this resolution. However, hon. members will surely understand that it would not be permissible for hon. members to cover the complete Income Tax Act.
It is my duty at the moment to ask hon. members to stay as close as possible to the relevant items under discussion. I, therefore, ask for their co-operation with respect to this particular matter. It is not my desire to call the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River to order on each matter he discusses. It would be appreciated if he stayed as close as possible to the items now under discussion.

I think you have given a ruling that is in accordance with our past practice. In the first place, at this stage one has not unlimited time. One is only provided with 30 minutes, and certainly one could not cover the whole of the Income Tax Act. In that respect, as you have ruled, one has the privilege, on a resolution of this kind, of referring to certain inadequacies. I was suggesting that this resolution is all the more inadequate because of certain expectations that had been aroused, not only in the minds of hon. members but of the general public, by the new Minister of Finance who was introducing this resolution.
I was about to indicate that he has pointed out in past days that not only did he believe that income tax exemptions should be raised from $1,000 to $1,500 for single people, but from $2,000 to $3,000 for married people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My friend is going right ahead to do the very thing you have ruled should not be done. The house has expressed itself on the very point to which my hon. friend insists on referring, the subject of exemptions. On June 26 the house divided
Income Tax Act
on an amendment to the main motion referring specifically to exemptions, and you will find the amendment in Votes and Proceedings, page 191. The amendment introduced by the hon. member for Assiniboia reads as follows:
This house further regrets that the government contemplates no action at this session to recognize the loss of purchasing power to the majority of Canadian citizens because of the lowered value of the dollar as related to consumer goods and prices, by amending the Income Tax Act so as to raise the amount of permissible income to single and married persons without taxation.
This last clause refers to exemptions and nothing else, Mr. Chairman. The house, in the division that occurred on June 26, which is recorded on pages 191 and 192 of Votes and Proceedings, negatived that motion. With respect I suggest that that negatives that matter and precludes discussion by the committee at this present session of parliament.

Mr. Chairman, suppose I, without prejudice, yield on that particular point. In the few minutes that are available to me I could discuss some other inadequacies which I shall proceed to. I want to refer to some other expectations that I think all of us would have expected to find in the first budget of a new administration by the Progressive Conservative party.
One of the things that I think is regrettable is that there was no reference in the resolution to the Income Tax Act being amended with respect to accelerated depreciation at this particular time of decline in our economy. There was circulation of a questionnaire among the business men of Canada or the business firms of Canada by the tax foundation not long ago and they replied that, next to a reduction in taxes itself, the form of tax relief they thought would be most helpful to the economy would be to give a capital cost allowance on an accelerated basis under present conditions. I wanted to point out to the house that this relief was in fact provided in the last budget in Great Britain. There was a 25 per cent increase with respect to capital cost allowances in the coming years, and particularly at the present time, to encourage new investment and to be a perk-up to the economy. We see nothing of that kind in the resolution in front of us.
I do not know whether the minister proposes to have a public review of the act we are discussing. However, we all know that when he sat on this side of the house that was one of the things that he consistently and persistently advocated. We thought that there might be in these resolutions something to indicate that the Income Tax Act was going to be amended to take care

Income Tax Act
of much that we have heard about giving Canadians opportunities equal to those of foreign investors in developing the country's natural resources. In the past we have heard much about overdeduction of taxes at source. We see nothing in the resolution with respect to that matter. My hon. friend may say that some of these things can be taken care of simply in regulations. But I would have thought that in the resolution that we have pertaining to the Income Tax Act, if Canadians could have some hopes of his carrying out some of the suggestions and promises that he has made in the past, we would have had by now some notice about it.
I found very recently that in the United Kingdom-and I referred to their budget a moment ago-some steps had been taken with respect to foreign investment. I am told that since 1947 profits paid by foreign-controlled concerns in the United Kingdom to their parent companies have been treated as undistributed profits and taxed at only 3 per cent. A wholly-owned subsidiary of a Canadian concern that had been paying the standard British corporation tax of 42.5 per cent plus the 3 per cent profits tax from the last budget of last spring would henceforth be subject to a tax of 52.5 per cent. I do not know whether or not the minister is giving consideration to that matter; but certainly up to now we have had no reference to it.
The colleagues of the Minister of Finance have urged repeatedly in this house that depreciation should be doubled. We are all the more surprised that something of this nature has not been done. In addition to that, we have had the Gordon report and the commission have made reference to certain changes in the Income Tax Act that they thought would be helpful to Canadian industry vis-a-vis foreign investment. We see nothing about that matter in the resolution now before us or in anything that we have had from the minister in the debate that took place previously.
We would have thought that we could have some confidence in expecting these things all the more when we heard about the platform of the Conservative party. When they had their last national convention in 1956 we read in the Ottawa Journal that the present hon. member for Calgary South, won his case at that convention when he called for an amendment to provide tax concessions for Canadian oil and gas operators equal to those obtained by United States operators from the United States government. We see nothing with respect to this matter in the budget resolution that we have before us. I believe the convention at that time went on record

as saying that they proposed to encourage national research by a more favourable tax climate. We read nothing about that matter in the budget resolutions nor is there anything from the other side to date in that respect.
The minister has indicated that this bill amending the Income Tax Act will probably be a substantial one. He was kind enough to tell me privately that it perhaps is the largest amending bill that the committee will have had before it for some time. I have no doubt that he will follow the practice of his predecessors and when presenting a bill of that consequence and intricacy, make it possible, not only for members of the house to be able to study its provisions but also the public. There is great advantage in not proceeding too quickly to second reading with respect to a mammoth bill of that kind because it is desirable that the public at large have an opportunity to learn of its provisions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I may assure my hon. friend that it is the intention to allow a sufficient period between first and second readings of the bill to afford hon. members as well as the interested public an opportunity to study the provisions of the bill.

We have a great number of new members. I think the house should be informed that there are some items which were referred to in the minister's budget speech-and which were, of course, given publicity in the press-but as to which we see no reference in the resolution before us. That is not contrary to custom by any means, Mr. Chairman. But one of these items is referred to at page 1243 of the minister's address. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, yes. An amendment to the act would be required for that purpose and the provision is contained in the bill.

I remember when the former minister of finance was making a speech about two years ago he paid some tribute to the former prime minister and the present Minister of Finance said that the whole reason for that speech was to praise the former prime minister. He quoted Lord Lyttleton to the effect that there is no weapon that slays its victims so surely as well aimed praise.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
May I ask the hon.
member if he wishes to speak generally or is the house now ready to go down paragraph by paragraph?

Generally. I recall that a previous resolution was introduced to this house recommending the removal of the
3	per cent floor in relation to the deductibility of medical expenses for income tax purposes and on that occasion the present Minister of Finance said the positions of the various parties in the house were well known and that so far as Her Majesty's loyal opposition was concerned its position was unchanged and that the opposition would support the resolution. He went on at considerable length to argue that medical expenses should be deducted, not only in respect to the amount in excess of 3 per cent of the taxable income, and at that time he gave the history of this legislation. He stated that the floor had been 5 per cent and after some years had been reduced to
4	per cent and then to 3 per cent, and I
Income Tax Act
know the hon. member for Hamilton West spoke at the same time in favour of the allowing of full medical expenses. Other hon. members who are now sitting on the treasury benches also supported the hon. lady's view, some of them including such expenses as transportation costs, nurses in the home, the conveying of patients from one point to another and many other expenses.
Paragraph 1 provides that amounts paid after June 17, 1958 for drugs and medicines which have been prescribed in writing by a medical practitioner be included in the medical expenses that are deductible in computing taxable income. I know of five or six drugs which are included in this category at the present time and I note that the bill provides for the inclusion of all drugs on prescription. In recent years new drugs, including particularly the broad spectrum of antibiotics, have been very expensive. In fact they cost from 50 cents to 75 cents a tablet, and a doctor does not need to give a prescription for many such tablets to make the bill run to $10 to $15. Many of our people, particularly those in the low income groups, cannot afford to pay these high prices.
Unfortunately this amendment does not help such people. It helps those in the middle and upper income groups. In my opinion it is just as necessary for low income groups to be provided with these special drugs, and I think the minister would be well advised to consider bringing down the cost of drugs, which he could do in a very simple way by eliminating the sales tax on drugs.
They could be regarded as a necessity of life.

Yes, I think such drugs are just as necessary as food in some cases because when there is a severe infection it is very necessary to have supplies of such antibiotics in order to save life.
The former minister of finance gave a $100 exemption to all those who did not have exemptions equalling that amount under charitable donations and medical expenses, and I am told that well over half our people came within this category. I notice that drugs must be prescribed in writing and I do know that a number of the non-narcotic drugs are prescribed over the telephone and that certain patients get repeat prescriptions several times during a year. I would like to ask the Minister of Finance whether in each case where drugs are purchased there must be a prescription and whether in the case of narcotic drugs the prescription would need to be

Income Tax Act
made in duplicate, since under our federal legislation the druggist must keep on file a copy of each prescription.
I know this would add very much to the extent of our bookkeeping systems. Those of us concerned with the field of medicine already have many forms to fill out and of course the druggists certainly have a great deal of bookkeeping of this nature. It would also add to the administrative responsibilities of the Department of National Revenue and we do not want to have too many new civil servants. We know that the Department of Finance, for instance, already has about 70 new employees this year-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not true.
How many are there?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I told you so two
weeks ago.
It may be only 69.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not true either.

It is right up there somewhere. This is the sort of thing about which the present Minister of Finance spoke when he complained of the wastefulness and extravagance in the various departments of government.
Paragraph 2 includes laboratory and other diagnostic services and I am just wondering how this might work out. At present some of these services are included in hospital and medical bills. If you pay a Blue Cross premium and you have a medical bill, say of $200, that $200 is considered as the amount allowable for deduction for income tax purposes.
Now, under the new Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act, the federal government will pay roughly one-half of the cost of treatment in our hospitals. It will pay one-half of the costs of the diagnostic and laboratory services in some provinces, but the other half would be paid by the patient himself in some provinces, or by some special tax levied in the provinces. I should like to ask the Minister of Finance what allowance would be made in future. Would the full hospital bill be allowed for deduction at present, or just the amount which a particular patient contributes by way of a premium? This is going to vary in the different provinces, and unless something is done you will have people in different parts of Canada paying on a different basis as far as income tax goes. Under paragraph 3, I think the government is providing:
That for 1958 and subsequent taxation years the maximum amount deductible by corporations for

contributions to charitable organizations be increased from 5 per cent of income to 10 per cent of income.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the hon. member would permit, I should like to suggest again, that it would contribute to an orderly discussion in committee if we approached this subject paragraph by paragraph. The hon. member, as I understood it, was making some general remarks but his remarks have all related to the first paragraph, and now he is going on to make remarks which relate to the third paragraph. I am saying the hon. member will have full opportunity to make his comments, but I suggest this should be done in an orderly way, the sections being discussed seriatim in the order in which they appear so that all hon. members who may wish to speak on a particular subject can do so during one period of time. Otherwise, we are bound to have a very discursive and disorderly discussion ranging over eight widely different matters which are mentioned in the eight different paragraphs.

I recall that in past years, after the general discussion had been concluded, there was universal agreement in the committee to proceed in that way. May I say to the minister, however, that in this particular case it happens that the hon. member for Welland, who is well informed on these matters, is anxious to speak on these subjects because instead of giving medical treatment, as is his usual practice, he will have to submit to medical treatment tomorrow and will not be free to make his remarks unless he can continue now.
I acquiesce to the minister's request.

Mr. Chairman, so many points of order have been raised that it is a little hard to know what is in order or not. We, of course, intend to support the resolution. The resolution is a most necessary one, and the principle is a good one.
The resolution seems to be in line with what was promised by the Prime Minister as reported in the Ottawa Journal of May 22, 1957, when he said the Conservative party would cut unnecessary taxation to promote production which would help meet the threat of inflation. Nowadays we might amend that to read: "to cut unnecessary taxation which would promote production which would help to relieve unemployment". However, that is another matter.
Then the Prime Minister added that last year the government had over-taxed the Canadian people by $500 million, and with this I come to the main theme of the remarks

I intend to make on this resolution, in that in our opinion the concession, welcome as it may be, is entirely inadequate. Not only is it inadequate, it falls far short of the pledge which was given the taxpayers of Canada.
On May 23, 1957, the Prime Minister claimed, as reported in the Vancouver Sun, that every Canadian man, woman and child had had their pockets picked by $30. This resolution is certainly not going to help that situation very much, and I am sure that the pockets of the taxpayers are going to continue to be picked. On May 24, 1957, the same hon. gentleman is reported to have said over a C.B.C. radio broadcast: "We will put an end to excessive over-taxation." Well, it is our opinion that this resolution, taken in its entirety, falls far short in its provisions of what is needed to relieve the people from over-taxation, and this is especially important at this moment when the time is overdue for the average people of Canada to be relieved of some of the burden of taxation in order that they may be able to buy more goods and hence provide more employment in Canada. I have in mind, for instance, the section of the resolution dealing with medical expenses.
While we welcome the extra concessions that are being made, we have over the years advocated the removal of the 3 per cent floor which presently exists, and if some bold and substantial measure of relief had been intended, that proposal might well have been given greater attention. I feel that with regard to medical expenses the act at the present time is needlessly cluttered up; one may deduct such medical expenses as exceed 3 per cent of net income, but one may not deduct such expenses as are in excess of a certain percentage of income. And then, if a person has no receipts at all he may deduct $100 for medical and charitable expenses, and so on. I, for one, would like to see all medical expenses for which receipts can be produced eligible for deduction. In this respect the resolution falls far short of expectations.
I know the house has voted on exemptions for single and married people, so I may not bring in my recommendations with regard to that; there will be another opportunity of doing so. However, the allowance for dependents falls far short of being realistic when considered in relation to present day cost of living. I believe no one in this committee would claim that a dependent child between the ages of 16 and 18, for instance, can be educated, clothed and looked after on an allowance of $500 a year, and I believe it is high time, especially in the light of higher education fees, that a substantial increase should be granted in this direction.
Income Tax Act
The minister spoke at some length with regard to the principle involved in raising the percentage of income which may be deducted in respect of contributions for charitable purposes. We agree that the needs of our institutions have risen with the years and the measure he has taken-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. If the hon.
member is going to talk on individual paragraphs I would ask him to withhold some of his remarks until the committee decides to deal with this resolution paragraph by paragraph.

It was not my intention to go into detail in my discussion of the individual subject. I meant only to survey these questions in order to show the inadequacy of the resolution as a whole. I certainly hope that this particular clause is not a reflection of the government's approach to the needs of education in Canada and especially the needs of higher education because it would be a sad day indeed if our educational institutions should have to rely for their continued successful operation and expansion on the proposed amendment to the Income Tax Act.
We regret very much that the government, among other things, has not seen fit to have listed a change in the social security tax that is presently paid under the Income Tax Act. At the present time a man having a taxable income of $3,000 pays $60 as a maximum in the form of a social security tax and the man having an income of $100,000 also pays a like amount. I feel that the minister might well have compensated the loss of revenue the government is sustaining by abolishing that maximum in order that people would pay into the social security tax fund according to their ability to pay.
In the main, we welcome the resolution. However, we must at this time remind the minister that it falls far, far short of what the people of this country had been led to believe they might expect and this takes on particular significance at this time when people require additional purchasing power to meet rising costs.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is the committee now prepared to discuss this resolution paragraph by paragraph?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall we now discuss paragraph one?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have an amendment to paragraph No. 1 which I shall ask one of my colleagues to introduce. The resolution at present contemplates in this paragraph that after the effective date amounts paid for drugs and medicines which

Income Tax Act
have been prescribed in writing by a medical practitioner may be included in the medical expenses that are deductible in computing taxable income. This matter has been reviewed and I should like to indicate that the proposed amendment is intended to provide that if drugs have been prescribed by a medical practitioner and recorded by a licensed pharmacist they may be included in the medical expenses that are deductible in computing taxable income. I would ask my colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, to move that amendment.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
It has been moved by Mr. Monteith (Perth) and seconded by Mr. Macdonnell:
That paragraph 1 of the income tax resolution be amended by deleting the words "in writing" and by adding the words "and recorded by a licensed pharmacist" immediately after the words medical practitioner in line 2 thereof.
The paragraph as amended will read:
That amounts paid after June 17, 1958, for drugs and medicines which have been prescribed by a medical practitioner and recorded by a licensed pharmacist be included in the medical expenses that are deductible in computing taxable income.
Shall the amendment carry?
Mr. Chairman, I take it that in no case is it necessary for the prescription, as such, to be sent in?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The prescription would be available for examination on the premises of the druggist, Mr. Chairman, and that would suffice.
But what about prescriptions for non-narcotic drugs that are simply phoned in?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Those prescriptions must be recorded. I mean by that that they are in practice, so this will come clearly within the terms of the amendment.
What evidence will be required of the individual taxpayer that expenditures have in fact been made, a receipt from the pharmacist or what?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, the receipt from the pharmacist under which he will have recorded the prescription.
That must be in writing, of course? There must be a written prescription recorded in the pharmacist's book?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister if every prescription must be recorded? For instance, a great many prescriptions are filled a dozen times or more on the basis of the original prescription. Would each prescription have to be included for each lot of medicine?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I take it that my hon. friend in his question is referring back to some of the designated drugs. With regard to those I may say that insulin, vitamin B12 and injectible liver extract are at present prescribed by a physician initially but it is usual for patients using those drugs to obtain them from their pharmacists without further reference to the initial prescription. Patients using those drugs know their dosage schedules and delays in obtaining requirements could, in some cases, prove fatal. It is intended that the amendment deal with these in such a way that receipts showing purchases of these three drugs need not have a prescription file number.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, when I first heard the amendment read I thought it made it easier to abide by the terms of paragraph one but now as I read it I think it makes it more difficult because what is necessary now in order to meet the terms of the first paragraph is that there must be a prescription by a medical practitioner and a recording by a licensed pharmacist. The two conditions must be there before the claim could be made, is that not right?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes; but you see, we are easing the requirement of the original resolution -because we are deleting the words "in writing" as applied to a prescription given by a medical practitioner. That takes care of the problem raised by the hon. member for Welland of the repeat order and the phone call.

Mr. Chairman, the person
requiring the prescription has no control over the druggist with regard to his recording it. He will enter a drugstore, present a prescription, receive it and leave and what the druggist does with respect to recording the prescription is something over which the customer has no control. It may not be recorded. The druggist may be careless or he may lose the prescription. The proposed amendment exposes the prospective user of that prescription to some difficulty. He may have a receipt but there may be no record of it in the drugstore through no fault of his own but through the fault of the druggist.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is obvious that if the individual in question wishes to claim the expenditure as a deduction by way of medical expenses he will have to be in a position to produce a receipt. Obviously when he makes a purchase he will have to see to it that what the law requires is done, both on his own part in obtaining a receipt and on the part of the druggist in recording it. That is only fair. I am quite sure my hon. friend does not expect the Department of National

Revenue to supply proof in these cases. The taxpayer will have to see to it that he preserves his receipts as he now does with respect to his other receipts that he intends to use for medical deductions.

The minister is perfectly right. I go along with that. The taxpayer will go in and buy and will get a receipt and go home, but from that moment he loses control over what transpires with the prescription behind the counter and in the druggist's office. He cannot go in there and watch to make sure that his prescription is recorded.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the committee adjourned at six o'clock we were discussing an amendment to paragraph 1 which reads as follows:
That paragraph 1 of the income tax resolution be amended by deleting the words "in writing" and by adding the words "and recorded by a licensed pharmacist" immediately after the words medical practitioner in line 2 thereof.
As amended will read:
That amounts paid after June 17, 1958, for drugs and medicines which have been prescribed by a medical practitioner and recorded by a licensed pharmacist be included in the medical expenses that are deductible in computing taxable income.
Shall the amendment carry?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps I should say just a word in reply to the question put by the hon. member for Cartier at six o'clock. The case he put, Mr. Chairman, is covered by the fact that the pharmacist has the record, for he must by law, keep a record of the sale. I think that is the complete answer to my hon. friend's question. He must do so as a matter of law.
I might add that this resolution and the amendment have been discussed with both the Department of National Health and Welfare and representatives of the Canadian pharmacists association. The amendment accords with the views that have been expressed by both of these sources.
I should like to know the mechanism that will be used under this amended section to claim the cost of drugs as a deduction. Must you send in the druggist's receipt plus the prescription?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The taxpayer does not send in the prescription to the Department of National Revenue when he files his income tax return. He sends in his receipt,
Income Tax Act
just as he does in connection with other elements in his claim for medical deduction, his receipt for the doctor's account, for the hospital account and others. He simply sends in his receipts, and the receipts will bear a reference to the prescription which is filed with the druggist.

If the drugs were ordered from the druggist by telephone, and the druggist made a note that they were ordered by telephone would the receipts given under those conditions be considered valid by the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, if the drugs in that case were, in fact, prescribed by the medical practitioner and were recorded by a licensed pharmacist, the cost of the drugs in that case would be treated as allowable medical deductions.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the amendment carry?

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Shall the clause as amended carry?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I take it, Mr. Chairman, you have put the amendment first. We are not adopting the paragraphs individually. As I understand it, there is only one resolution before the committee and there is only one motion for adoption of the resolution which will be put after we have gone through the eight paragraphs. An amendment at any time would have to be put.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If I understand the discussion aright, the amendment has now carried. It is the intention to dispose of this resolution clause by clause, so the amendment having carried is the clause still open for discussion?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Probably my friend did not hear the discussion this afternoon. There is only one resolution before the committee. This one resolution has eight paragraphs to it. It was agreed this afternoon that in the interests of orderly discussion the paragraphs should be called seriatim and the discussion in each case would necessarily be relevant to the particular paragraph. At the conclusion, one motion would be put for adoption of the resolution as amended.
Amendments, of course, could be introduced to any paragraph at any time. I take it that if there is no further discussion sought on paragraph 1, then the chairman would now be calling paragraph 2.

I was under a misapprehension. I thought probably the amendment was being put to regularize the paragraph. I should like to ask a few more questions on item No. 1.

Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As amended.
As amended. Could the minister indicate to us just what he estimates will be the cost to the treasury of both paragraph 1 and paragraph 2?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: From $4 million to $5 million.
In a full fiscal year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In a full fiscal year.

If we do, finally dispose of paragraph 1, we automatically go on to paragraph 2 and so on to paragraph 8, and take one vote. Does that leave the door open, while we are at paragraph 5, for someone to revert to paragraph 1 if he so desires?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I take it that would mean chaos in our proceedings. What was agreed upon this afternoon, in the general interests of orderly discussion, was that each paragraph would be called seriatim. If there is no further discussion, then the chairman will proceed to call the next paragraph. The discussion on the previous paragraph would then have been exhausted and closed.
I agree with you on that. I was just asking for clarification of the procedure.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is there further discussion on paragraph 1?

Yes. I was interested in hearing the remarks of the hon. member for Welland. I thought they were well taken. I am sure that he knows his suggestion with respect to the elimination of sales tax on drugs was last month endorsed by a very important organization, the national council of women.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: With respect, Mr. Chairman, we are not discussing the sales tax now. We are discussing the amendment to the Income Tax Act, and the sales tax on drugs is surely not relevant.

That is correct, but my next point was going to be that any concession that might be made from the point of view of foregoing revenue might be better done this way because, as the hon. member for Welland indicated, there are a great number of people who are not taxpayers. Those, of course, are the more poorly off people of the country. This measure does not provide them with any benefit so far as their expenditures for drugs are concerned. I may be one year out of date but I have here readily available the 1956 tax statistics, and I think they have reference to the 1954 tax returns. There one
will find that the taxable returns were 3,410,160 and the non-taxable returns were 1,393,250. In addition to that, of course, a number of people are not even called upon to put in a return. I just wanted to commend the hon. member for Welland for his remarks. He, of course, referred to the fact that he too was surprised that this resolution had not gone further. I find that at least on a number of occasions in recent years the Minister of Finance associated himself with his party in indicating in his vote in this house that he felt the floor itself should be removed. I refer to the vote on January 30, 1956; the vote on February 14, 1955; and the vote on January 18, 1954.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: With the exception of that last date my hon. friend voted against the proposal on each occasion and his party did so also.

My hon. friend may be talking about consistency but I am simply pointing out to him that we expected some consistency from him when he on three occasions indicated to the public at large this was something about which he felt vehemently and on those occasions voted that the floor be removed. As the hon. member for Welland has indicated, either that procedure or the elimination of the sales tax would be more beneficial than the resolution we have before us tonight.

Mr. Chairman, I am concerned about part of this resolution. I believe the minister will know what I am speaking about as I have already drawn the matter to his attention. I refer to the wording of this resolution which has to do with the deduction of medication for income tax purposes. I spoke about the matter previously. I should like to draw to the attention of the minister and his department that the resolution, as it is worded, says "prescribed in writing" or words to that effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether my hon. friend has just come into the chamber. I may tell him that the resolution has been amended. I think the amendment fully covers the point my hon. friend has in mind.
I thank the minister. That is all that I was concerned about.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is there any further discussion on paragraph 1?
Carried.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall we proceed to paragraph 2?
Agreed.

In connection with paragraph 2 I have a question. When the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act is in operation, as it is now in parts of Canada, I should like to know what part of the hospital bill will be deductible in respect of income tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The entire bill, just as at present. The statute to which my hon. friend has referred has not changed the situation, and the Income Tax Act is not being amended in that respect. The position is just the same as if today the taxpayer's hospital account was paid by his insurance company.

Then it means that they would get the part that the federal government pays, Vhich is roughly 50 per cent of the treatment in the general hospital. They will be able to deduct that part in respect of their income tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not what I said, Mr. Chairman. I said that the hospital account would be admissible just as at present if it were paid by an insurance company. There is no change in the position in that respect. I am not saying what the situation might be or what the new situation brought about by the act may call for later on. But as things stand now, no change is made in the law in that respect.

That act is in operation now in certain provinces in Canada. I should like to know what will happen in connection with taxpayers making claims in those provinces, and whether the total hospital bill would be presented or just the part that was not paid by the dominion government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Whatever the account is, as rendered to the taxpayer, and is paid. Under the provisions of the new act, whatever that hospital account is it is treated just as is the hospital account today that is paid on behalf of the taxpayer by his insurance company. I cannot put it any more clearly than that.

Suppose no account is
rendered to the patient in hospital and his bill is paid half by the federal government and the other half by the provincial government where the money is raised say by a sales tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In order to have the benefit of a deduction he must be in a position to produce a receipted hospital account.
And it must be more than 3 per cent of his income.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. But what I mean is that in order to qualify at all, he
57071-3-134
Income Tax Act
must be able to produce a receipted hospital account in the case put by my hon. friend. It is not everybody who will be under the scheme in any of the provinces in which the new systems come into effect on July 1. What the method will be in any particular province I would not be prepared to say now, or as to the practice of the hospital; but if he produces a receipted hospital account, a bona fide account duly receipted, then it will qualify as a medical expense.

That would therefore mean that in certain provinces where he pays a premium, he might pay half his hospital account; and in another province where the province is contributing the whole thing he would be presented with no hospital account. Hence people in different provinces would be treated differently.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no province now of which I am aware that is paying the entire cost. Those provinces that had hospital insurance schemes are the ones that are coming in now under the provisions of the new act with effect from July 1.

In the province of British Columbia, where I believe the hospital scheme is paid for in large part by a retail sales tax of 5% levied by the province, is it possible for a resident to submit his hospital bills if he requires hospitalization in the course of the year and it appears worth while in that these bills with the other medical bills, go beyond 3 per cent of his income.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not the method of the payment of the premium under the provincial scheme that governs whether the hospital account is a deductible medical expense. It is whether the hospital renders an account and the taxpayer is in a position to produce a receipted account. In that particular case the yield from the sales tax, of course, is turned over to those responsible for operating the hospital scheme. But that is not the determining factor in relation to the test of eligibility of the account to rank as a medical expense.

I do not quite understand my hon. friend. Let us consider the situation that has existed up until now in the province of Ontario where I think probably 75 per cent of the wage earners are now enrolled in Blue Cross.
Blue Cross is an organization supported by premiums which more or less equal the outgo in respect of all accounts presented to Blue Cross by the hospitals. It has been my understanding that an individual has never been able to render to the Department of National Revenue for deduction from income

Income Tax Act
tax the cost as a medical expense his premium, but if he does require hospitalization the hospital does not render him an account and he does not have to pay anything. But he can go, to the hospital and ask for a statement of what the charges would have been had he not been insured, and it is that statement which is submitted to the Department of National Revenue. This was why I raised the query with respect to British Columbia where there is no exact fixed premium but there is of course the retail sales tax which is supposed to support the hospitals in that province, or has been supposed to do so up until now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: At the risk of repetition, may I say that it is the receipted account which is the prerequisite, indeed the test of eligibility for an account to rank as a medical expense. It is not the premium, however collected or however paid, which is the determining factor. Indeed for this purpose it is not relevant. It is the receipted account of the hospital that governs the decision.

I would like to refer to the language of this paragraph which refers to transportation to or from a hospital by ambulance which may be included under medical expenses. Perhaps the minister may be able to give some clarification on this point having regard to the following situations which might arise. One can easily conceive, for example, that someone in, say Seven Islands has an accident and must be rushed to hospital by plane. A plane is not necessarily an ambulance but it could perhaps be called an ambulance for this purpose. Secondly, there may be a case where a plane would have to go to a place such as Sudbury on the instructions of the doctor treating a patient there in order to transport the patient to Montreal for treatment. Even though such a patient is not transported by ambulance such a conveyance might be called an ambulance in this case also. Then there is a third possibility, where a person has to be rushed to hospital and there is no ambulance, as such, available.
Would the transportation in each of the three cases to which I have referred be covered?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The answer in all three cases is no.

May I ask the minister what would be the position in a case where there is a regular air ambulance service as there is in the province from which I come? Such service, as the minister well knows, has saved a great many lives. It is a standard service and has been in operation for more than ten years. There is a registered nurse on the

plane at all times and all the facilities are available which would be available in an ambulance, including those for the administration of oxygen when necessary.
It seems to me that in such an instance an air ambulance service is just as much an ambulance service as it would be if it were on four wheels on the ground. I would think the minister would not wish to place the federal government in the position where it would deny the cost of a service which is, and for some time past has been, largely although not wholly subsidized by the provincial government. The person who is being transported is charged a flat fee, which varies in one or two minor ways but is in the neighbourhood of $25 to $35. After the air ambulance lands at the airporj a regular ambulance, the automobile variety, picks up the patient and takes him to the hospital.
The cost of the automobile ambulance is a few dollars less than the $25 to $35 charge for the air ambulance service but in view of the fact that this air service is a regular one-it is very definitely an ambulance- assisting in the saving of many, many lives,
I feel the minister should favourably consider this request.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not possible for me to give a categorical answer to my hon. friend, but I think in many instances an airplane could not in any sense be regarded as an ambulance. If, however, such an airplane is equipped and used for no other purpose than the transportation of the sick, maimed or injured, then I would think the Department of National Revenue would be disposed to look favourably on such a case, provided it were properly substantiated. I emphasize, however, that the plane must be confined with respect to its equipment and use to that purpose and to no other.

Emergency situations might arise which would cause the plane to be used perhaps once or twice a year for some other purpose but this is a regular service and the plane at least 99 times out of 100 is used for the purposes of transportation of patients only. The plane will not take off unless a doctor has ordered the plane to pick up a patient at some outlying point and unless that doctor already has available a bed in the hospital for such patient. I would therefore think such a proposition would be on all fours with one concerning any other ambulance service.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If those are the circumstances I think the Department of National Revenue would rule such a plane to be an ambulance.

I thank the minister very much for his answer. I see he has been in consultation with the Minister of National Revenue who probably knows that this is a regular service on a province-wide basis. I believe anyone receiving a bill from the Saskatchewan air ambulance service, on the face of it, has a bona fide claim under this paragraph.

I am wondering if the
minister's negative answer to the three questions I put to him is altogether in fulfilment of the spirit prompting this legislation, especially if the legislation is indeed intended to offer relief from stress caused by illness. The language used is "transportation to or from a hospital". It does not speak of transportation within any limits, and if it was intended to restrict the coverage to certain areas the wording should be
within a radius of 50 miles from a hospital" or "20 miles" or some other distance.
Since the proposed legislation does not specify a limit to the distance over which an invalid may be transported then I think the minister should perhaps reconsider his answer. One can easily conceive that even an automobile ambulance might have to transport a patient over a distance of 300 or 500 miles. Would such a case be covered?
I do not see that any citizen who finds it impossible to obtain an ambulance, in the sense that we understand the word-fully equipped and on four wheels-should be prejudiced in any way by this lack of transportation, or because no roads are available.
I do not think such a citizen should suffer because the only means of transport is by air, and I think the minister might give some consideration to the merit of allowing the deduction to a person who has to be transported to hospital in this way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I can assure the hon. member that the minister has a big and sympathetic heart with regard to these considerations, and I only wish he had spoken as forcefully when he was sitting on this side of the house in support of a proposal to offer some relief to those who incur expenditure through being transported to or from hospitals. This is the first time in the history of Canadian income tax legislation that any legislative proposal has been put before parliament for permitting any form of transportation expense to be included as a deduction for income tax purposes. This is the first time.
We cannot include every form of transportation; the difficulties of administration and enforcement would be almost insuperable if this provision were thrown wide open. If expenditure on, say, taxis were to be
57071-3-134J
Income Tax Act
allowed I do not know how you would effectively enforce the act, because who is going to check all these cases? We considered all aspects of the matter and came to the conclusion that limitation of the vehicle was the only effective means of fair and adequate enforcement of the regulations by the officers of the Department of National Revenue, It will be the nature of the vehicle used to transport the patient to and from hospital which will determine whether the expenditure qualifies under this provision.

Having listened carefully to the minister's answers to repeated questions I do want to say that he has deeply failed on this occasion to use the English language with his usual exactitude. When we want to find out the meaning of the words which the minister uses in his eloquent and vehement speeches we are in the habit of referring to dictionaries in order to get his meaning, and the same is true when it comes to an act. If you want to understand an act you look in a dictionary. I have looked in a dictionary to find out the meaning of the word "ambulance", and the dictionary describes it as "a conveyance for sick and wounded persons". So unless there is a further definition added, I am convinced that if someone challenged a case before the courts the judge would have to refer to the Oxford dictionary or to some accepted dictionary in order to find out the meaning of the word. I think the word used here is far too broad, and that without further definition it would create misunderstanding.
In addition, I cannot see why the allowance should be confined to ambulances of a certain type, because we have so many instances in this country where it is not possible to get the normal type of ambulance when sickness or accidents occur. I am glad to see that the Minister of National Revenue has his ears cocked my way. The hon. member for Cartier has mentioned one such instance. In the area from which I come we often have to use water taxis or launches in order to convey injured persons over long stretches of water to hospitals. Surely, a person who has to incur considerable expense in this way should be in the same position as one who takes an ambulance' for a mile or two in a city. In addition, we have such a thing as horse ambulances because roads are often not good enough to-enable us to get out men who have been injured and, on other occasions, I remember that pack and saddle horses have been used to get men to hospital from mountain tops.
I suggest, then, that the term now used is far too broad and that the minister's replies

Income Tax Act
are not related to the dictionary definition o 1 the word "ambulance". I think he is in for a lot of trouble unless he adds some interpretation to the legislation. In addition, I want to emphasize that I cannot see the fairness of confining this to cases where a particular type of ambulance is used, mostly over paved roads and for short distances, while the people who live in the backwoods, the people who work in the mines and mills and woods and who produce a great deal of the natural wealth which keeps the wheels of industry in this country turning are unfairly dealt with.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: I am fully in agreement with the remarks which have been made by the hon. member for Kootenay West. In the district in which I live we have a very good hospital and we have very good doctors. However, on many occasions a doctor will be unable to perform an operation and patients have to be sent to Toronto. In such cases patients are sent on doctor's orders and they have to travel either by train or by air. It is a very costly trip, representing a journey of 575 miles, and if this act is intended to give relief to the taxpayers it seems to me it should apply to transportation of this kind as well, unless the minister wants to make a big impression with a little concession.

Mr. Chairman, in Newfoundland and in many parts of northern Newfoundland and Labrador the air ambulance is the only kind of ambulance there is, and the government of Newfoundland has purchased suitable aircraft for use in taking patients to hospital in an emergency. Despite the existence of these official air ambulances it is necessary at times to use planes and helicopters which are normally engaged on other work. I should like to think that people transported in such aircraft being used as ambulances will come within the provisions of the act.

I am quite sure the minister knows that there are hundreds of villages in Canada where there are no ambulances at all. An invalid might have to be transported from one village to a neighbouring village, a little larger, where there is some hospital service. A citizen who hires a taxi or who rents an automobile, or a conveyance of some kind, and who has to spend a certain sum of money should surely be entitled to deduct that expenditure even though, strictly speaking, he did not use a vehicle with a red cross on it marked with the word "ambulance". I think that is the intention of this amendment. The intention is to confer a benefit on people so that they may have certain advantages
[Mr. Herridge.l
with respect to medical expenses being deducted, and it should not be so restricted as to apply in practice only to people who live in cities where ambulances are available; it should confer an equal benefit on all Canadian citizens.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have already explained to my hon. friend why, after very careful consideration, it was found not possible to extend this benefit more widely. The difficulties of enforcement were found to be insuperable. If the committee wants that point met and if the objection is going to be pressed it may be that my hon. friends will just talk the taxpayer out of getting this opportunity to have a deduction with respect to expenditures made on ambulances because I can assure the hon. gentleman that this and the other questions he has raised were very carefully considered and the difficulties in the way of enforcement were found to be insuperable.

Mr. Chairman, I can tell the minister that as far as my riding is concerned there is no ambulance. In order for a person in a remote area to get to a hospital he must hire a taxi and travel anywhere from 80 to 100 miles or he must hire a boat and travel 50 or 60 miles at considerable expense. No one in my riding can benefit from this proposal. I do not think we should put on our statute books legislation that discriminates between one taxpayer and another. We should treat all taxpayers alike.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to point something out to the minister with which I think he will agree. In paragraph No. 1 the minister was ingenious enough to find a method of designating what medical expenses can be deducted. He placed, as it were, an identity card upon those drugs which can be deducted when he established that they must be procured by prescription from a physician. I believe a means of identification could be found in the present instance, too. If the law were to read that the vehicle was deemed necessary by a duly qualified practitioner and that it was required for an emergency and should therefore be a deductible expense, that would be a means of identifying it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
All I can suggest to my hon. friend, Mr. Chairman, is that he give us a chance to work this proposal out on the present basis. In time we will see what we can do. We started out to try to help the taxpayer by this means. We have gone as far as we can see the possibility of effective enforcement in the measure before us. All I can suggest in the face of that is that we are trying to help the taxpayer who incurs

expense in being transported to a hospital. I urge hon. gentlemen opposite to give it a trial and provide an opportunity for the department to work with it and we will see what can be done. That is all I can suggest to my hon. friends under the present circumstances.
That is fair enough.

Mr. Chairman, we all commend the minister for taking this forward step with respect to transportation for the sick but may I point out that it is not unusual at this stage in the discussion of budget resolutions for the Minister of Finance to be impressed with a suggestion receiving support from hon. members all across the house and the administration reconsiders the bill. This suggestion certainly has an appeal to me on the basis of its reasonableness. It is not at all unusual to amend a proposed bill on the floor. I think the minister could go one step further than just saying, "Let us examine it in another year." Between now and second reading of the bill I believe that he and his officials could examine this proposal and bring in a measure that is considerably more likely to equate the situation for all people across Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if the suggestion were new I should have no hesitation at all in acceding to my hon. friend's proposal but I repeat that it is not new. We considered this matter in all its ramifications very carefully and, I might add, at very great length. Here we have gone as far as we can see the effective limits of enforcement. I do not think I can do more than suggest what I suggested to hon. members earlier in reply to the last remarks of my friend the hon. member for Cartier.

Mr. Chairman, could I offer another suggestion to the minister. When he calculated the amount that this measure would cost the treasury he must have had in mind some average figure representing the cost of an ambulance, perhaps $15 or $20. Why not put a similar limit on with respect to deductibility and let everyone who incurs expenses benefit to that extent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
that does not overcome the problem of enforcement in regard to somebody who takes a taxi ride. You cannot enforce a provision that is related to a taxi ride; that is just the difficulty.

But surely the hospital
authorities could certify the expenditure?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hospital does not pay the taxi driver.
Income Tax Act

Mr. Chairman, could I put this question to the minister. Would it be on a par with past practice if the doctor added the cost of transportation to his bill and rendered it to the patient in the same way as in the past we know that doctors have provided drugs and added the cost to their bill? Such expenditures were recognized for tax deduction by the taxation division of the Department of National Revenue.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid it is not analagous to the cost of a prescription for which I argued for many a long year and with respect to which my hon. friend and those associated with him would not accede.

My hon. friend knows that the former administration took a very careful look at the question of drugs and because of the argument that drugs were an important item of medical expenditure it deliberately lowered the floor from 5 per cent to 4 per cent stating at the time that it was doing so for the purpose of recognizing that about 1 per cent of medical expenditures of this nature on average were for drugs. Also the then administration made it clear that in doing so the administration was saving the taxpayer a lot of money by not having officials examine small accounts and conduct correspondence about them.

Mr. Chairman, I like the way this particular paragraph reads just as it is and I think it should remain in this form because when you take a ride in an ambulance you have more than transportation, you also receive medical attention. I should like to see the word "licensed" inserted before the word "ambulance" in this paragraph. As hon. gentlemen probably know, we have a very good hospital plan in the province of Saskatchewan.
Hear, hear.

I expected this would draw applause and particularly from hon. members of the C.C.F. group and those from Saskatchewan. We are all proud of the plan we have there. We also have a splendid air ambulance service which will go into any part of the province. May I suggest to those hon. members who have been wondering what they can do in their part of the country and how they could benefit under the terms of this measure that they should perhaps try to establish an air ambulance service in their areas as well.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Maybe a good C.C.F. government would be a solution.

Income Tax Act
The people of the province of Saskatchewan wanted it and we do not think the C.C.F. should claim all the credit for it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It is the only province that has it.
I should like to see it left as it is and I know that the people of Saskatchewan will welcome it as just one more forward step taken by this government for the benefit of Canadians.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if in considering this the minister and his officials really did consider the back areas of the country where there are vast distances to cover. It is all right for the minister to say that there are difficulties involved in keeping track of taxi fares but that is not a satisfactory answer. The country in northern and northwestern Ontario and other parts of Canada has been famous for its mercy flights. Hundreds of families have been assisted in bringing out people from distant parts who require urgent medical attention. In all common sense I cannot see why this sort of flight which is made at a tremendous expense to the patient or his parents could not be checked and certified by a doctor or hospital authority. The provision before us may be all very fine for the people in Crest-wood Heights but it does not do anything for people in places along the northshore area or in the bush country.
Where is Crestwood Heights?

It is a figment of some sociologist's imagination. It is in North Toronto not very far from where the minister comes. As a matter of fact, a very interesting book has been written about it and you might get more of an idea, Mr. Chairman, about the background of the hon. member for Eglinton if you had a look at it. That is getting away from the point. This matter should be gone into more thoroughly and a more attractive answer or reason given than the one the minister presented.

If I may go back to hospital charges I should like to ask one question. Suppose a person now goes to a hospital in Ontario and is covered by Blue Cross. If he has a bill of $300 Blue Cross will pay the bill and the patient will get the receipt. Suppose the same thing happens after January 1 next when the Ontario hospital insurance scheme comes into effect. Will the department accept a receipt in full for $300 or will they only accept a receipt for about $150 because the federal government will be paying about half the hospital bill? Suppose we take Saskatchewan where there are no direct contributions
IMr. Peters.]
in the form of premiums. What would the department accept there in the case of a patient with the same number of hospital days, the same services and the same charge? Would they get their $300 just the same?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I must point out that this matter was fully discussed and I answered that question as fully and as adequately as I can when my hon. friend asked it four or five times half an hour ago. I point out also that the question does not arise under the present paragraph at all. If my hon. friend is not content with the answer I gave him earlier then I think it is a case where probably he can communicate with the Department of National Revenue. It is something which does not arise out of these amendments at all.

I do not begrudge at all to the minister credit for the improvements made under clause 2 of the resolution. I note with pleasure that eyeglasses are one of the expenditures that from now on may be included if a person's total expenditures exceed three per cent of his income. But looking at it in a practical way I think that people are going to have to break a lot of eyeglasses for this to mean very much. The hon. member for Welland indicated that he thought that perhaps 50 per cent of the taxpayers would get no benefit from this section because they would be benefiting under the standard $100 exemption made available last year in Mr. Harris' budget.
I would go further and ask whether the minister would quarrel with an estimate I have in my mind that the percentage of taxpayers with less than $100 claimed for such deductions in the past and who would thus utilize the standard exemption would not be 50 per cent but nearer to 70 per cent. I notice that the Minister of National Revenue, the minister's colleague in these budget matters, is sitting next to the minister. From reading the newspapers a lot of people think that the exemption with respect to eyeglasses means that the total cost of the eyeglasses will come off their income tax bill. That, of course, is not the case. Their income tax rate would be what would determine what portion they would save on the total cost of the glasses.
In the first income taxable range the tax rate is 15 per cent so in that case they would only save 15 per cent of the cost of the glasses. It has come to the attention of all of us, that during the time the Minister of National Revenue has assumed duties of tax collection, that in Vancouver, as we were sorry to learn, something in the nature of a kickback system has been in operation involving the purchase of glasses. As I recall

the circumstances the kickback to the doctors was unknown to the purchasers of glasses and amounted to anywhere from 25 per cent to 33i per cent of the cost of the glasses.
Therefore I say that while there might be a 15 per cent saving for somebody whose total expenditures were over three per cent of his income, nevertheless it would only apply to 30 per cent of our total taxpayers. If the Minister of National Revenue can assure us he is looking into this situation on a nationwide basis I think that is probably the best thing we can do for most people who are obliged to buy glasses.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I think the hon. member can accept my assurance in that respect, that the matter is being fully investigated across Canada.
Could the minister tell us whether the cost of earphones for people who are hard of hearing is deductible?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are already allowed under the act and have been for some time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Clause 3.

I am particularly happy that under this clause the minister has increased the exemption for contributions to charitable organizations from five per cent to ten per cent. He himself referred to the great need of universities and colleges for additional money. We all know that with the increasing need for additional classroom space, equipment, more money for salaries for professors and so on, this can be a very helpful provision. I should like to ask the minister one or two questions. In his budget address he said, as found on page 1244 of Hansard of June 17:
-far too many corporations do not come close to taking advantage of the present five per cent limit; but I am glad to say that many corporations do take their responsibilities in these matters seriously.	,
He was making the point that under this provision private Canadian corporations can make greater contributions to universities and colleges. That is particularly important in the province of Quebec where in effect government gifts without strings attached are, I think we can assume, not altogether popular at the moment. Therefore private enterprise will have to make up the difference to meet the tremendous needs of colleges and universities in the immediate future.
My first question is: Has the minister any figures or is he able to give us any percentage of Canadian corporations which do contribute under this provision? Second, would the minister tell us what "charitable organizations" means? Can he define it? I am well
Income Tax Act
aware that section 62 (1) (e) of the act defines it to a certain degree but would the term "charitable organizations" apply to charitable trusts, non-profit corporations, low cost housing corporations, provincial governments and Canadian municipalities. I also understand that the 1957 amendment permitted the excess of donations over five per cent, now ten per cent, to be deducted the following year. Does this still remain in force?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
On the first point, Mr. Chairman, according to the statistics for the last year available, 1956, corporations contributed in round figures $32 million to charitable organizations within the meaning of the Income Tax Act, and that was one per cent of their income. On the average they have not been contributing up to the five per cent. Some have, and encouragement is being given, we hope, by the proposed amendment to all corporations to contribute more generously to the support of charitable organizations.
On the second point, there is no change brought about by the proposed amendment in the definition of "charitable organizations" under section 62 (1) (e) of the act.
On the third point, the matter of carrying forward, the answer is yes, the carry-forward still obtains.

During his budget speech the minister said that the increase from 5 per cent to 10 per cent was given especially to help education. If I recall well, he said that evening that educational institutions were counting too much on the government and private corporations had to do their share. I see by the wording of the amendment that the exemption for contributions to charitable organizations by corporations is to be increased from 5 per cent to 10 per cent. If it was the intention of the minister that this money should go for education, why did he not make special provision for a 10 per cent deduction for contributions to education and a 5 per cent deduction for other charitable purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I made a special plea to corporations to give support to education through universities for a particular reason, but I did not suggest that the purpose for which the act now recognizes a deduction should be confined to gifts to universities. I did indicate in my budget speech that the deduction would apply in the case of gifts to charitable organizations. The one change this resolution would make in the act would be to change the one figure, the figure 5 to the figure 10.
Hon. members are aware that strong efforts have been made, in the last several years

Income Tax Act
particularly, to put before corporations a plea that they recognize their responsibility in a special degree in connection with university education, and particularly corporations engaged in technical pursuits. A strong plea has been made to them by many enterprises of a philanthropic nature to assist in education. I think that while this amendment does not attempt to narrow in any way the definition of charitable organizations under the act, nevertheless there is reason to hope that corporations will look with particular favour on the plea that they support, through charitable donations in their normal budgets, university education.
There are obvious reasons. Corporations are not subject in the same way as individuals to pleas for support for ordinary church or religious works, and many corporations do not feel disposed to contribute, as individuals do, to the support of church and religious organizations but those corporations will, nevertheless, respond to an appeal to contribute to the assistance of university education.
If I understood the minister correctly, I believe he said that the corporations of our country have contributed but one per cent towards these charitable institutions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not a good enough record.
I was going to say that that certainly is not very commendable. In other words, they had a latitude of an additional four per cent of which they did not take advantage.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Many of them did not.

I am speaking of the average. I am wondering whether the addition of five per cent would merely widen the margin of deficiency, of neglect or carelessness or avoidance of responsibility. I am wondering whether or not that would give them much encouragement because, in my judgment, they are extremely delinquent in complying with the possibilities.
What I say may be a bit drastic, Mr. Chairman, but I am wondering whether or not the law could not be changed to compel corporations to take full advantage of that exemption. If, for example, a tax were imposed on corporation profits to the extent of five per cent-I will not go as high as the ten per cent which the minister suggests-the revenue from that tax could be used to create a fund to be distributed amongst educational and charitable institutions. In other words, we could compel corporations of this country to take advantage of the possible exemption.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think my hon. friend will agree with me that the penalty imposed on corporations by the law today for not contributing up to the permissible percentage to charitable organizations is pretty heavy. It is 47 per cent, and that is a very stiff kind of penalty to impose. I think my hon. friend will agree with me on that.
That is the perfect answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In the second
place, I think the increase from five per cent to 10 per cent in the permissible percentage will have the effect for which he and I are arguing. In the first place, there are some corporations that do today contribute up to the full permissible five per cent, and would contribute more if the law permitted them to do so without penalty. In those cases, certainly there will be more generous contributions in view of the proposed increase from five per cent to ten per cent. But in addition, I think in the case of those corporations which have not been contributing hitherto up to the full permissible five per cent there will now be greater consciousness of the opportunity that is given to them and the social responsibility that goes with it. It may well be that some corporations have fought shy of some charitable appeals on the theory that they might, somehow or other, at the end of the year be crowding their five per cent. They will not be quite so apprehensive in the late months of the year of crowding ten per cent. I have some hope that more corporations, and I tried to put it rather strongly in the budget speech, will now recognize their social responsibilities in this respect.
It might be just as well to point out that before we force corporations to contribute up to five per cent or ten per cent we should make sure that they have profits of five per cent or ten per cent.

Since 1941 there has been a standard spread between the allowable charitable deduction with respect to individuals of 10 per cent and corporations at five per cent. I was wondering why, when he was raising the maximum deduction in case of corporations, he did not see fit to do likewise also in the case of individuals. The minister in his remarks indicated that he felt individuals had appeals for religious and local charitable donations that were not so regularly accepted by corporations. 1 suggest to him that perhaps the individual has both, he has the appeal for capital requirements for educational institutions as well as the steady annual religious and local type of appeals that are made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think that under the present circumstances one could depart from the historical, biblical conception of the tithe. I understand that was always the basis of the 10 per cent figure applied to charitable donations under the act for individuals. In the case of corporations, we are simply bringing them up on a level with the position of the individual.
