The tithing principle is recognized now by the act with respect to all taxpayers, whether individual or corporations.
On the second point, I may tell my hon. friend that while it may be that there are more types of charitable appeals to individuals than to corporations, the record again of the average figure for the individual is not as impressive as perhaps most of us in this house would wish.
In the year 1956 the total of charitable donations of individuals reported in income tax returns was $248 million which happens to be 2 per cent of the income of the individuals.
What is the corporation record?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The corporation record in that year was one per cent of income.

In his budget speech the minister said that the majority of corporations did not use the 5 per cent already admissible for exemption. How can he expect that they are going to use the 10 per cent that is to be exempted?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I endeavoured to answer that question when it was asked by hon. members opposite. I do not think I can usefully add to what I have already said. If they do not use it, they will pay in tax 47 per cent of what they have not chosen to contribute to charity up to 10 per cent of income.

Perhaps I could simply suggest to my hon. friend that I think he has indicated agreement with the development of the last administration in allowing a little bit of averaging. But the averaging is for a relatively short period, from one year to the next. As time goes on I think he may find that too many taxpayers are not giving adequately, either on the personal side or the corporation side, for fear that their income for the coming year is not ascertained. It might be to the benefit of all society if the averaging period were extended to perhaps two years or three years or something like that and they were then less cautious and gave more generously.

I wonder whether the minister could tell the house just how many firms 57071-3-135
Income Tax Act
or corporations have contributed the full 5 per cent or what per cent of the corporations have contributed fully?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are no available statistics on that point, I am informed.

We realize very well the urgent need of our institutions, especially in the field of education, for additional resources at this time. I do not want to do anything that is going to make contributions to them any less, either the contributions of individuals or the contributions of corporations, however, as I indicated before the dinner recess, I sincerely hope that this is not an approach that is going to be used, or a major approach even, to the very urgent problem being faced by our higher institutions of learning. I am all in favour of individuals exercising charity. However, I am a little bit leery when a huge corporation professes to do so because there is not very much heart in that type of a gift. It is a fairly coldblooded proposition when a huge corporation makes a donation to a charitable organization; and very often that definitely is the case when it makes a donation to a higher institute of learning. We had the evil practice beginning in the province of British Columbia whereby the local grants are based on the amount of money the university is able to raise by way of donations. I should hate to see the day come when the federal government begins to institute any taxation system whereby they will make any payment to education dependent upon the payment being made by huge corporations.
When these corporations make these grants, especially in the scientific field, to our higher institutions of learning they are not acting entirely from unselfish motives. Therefore the expression "charitable organizations" mentioned in the resolution begins to lose a little bit of its real validity. These organizations will make their grants to universities and will attach riders to the grants and make them conditional upon the money donated being used for specific purposes at the university. That leaves the whole field of research open to some very serious questioning.
For many long years now we have taken rather great pride in the liberty attached to our educational institutions. While I am willing to admit that an individual making a donation to a university-I think this can be fairly said-is not able, even if he wished to do so, to exercise any undue influence upon that university, however, when a university is brought into the position where it is obliged to rely for any large share of its revenue upon the contributions of huge corporations, *-and they are becoming larger every year-

Income Tax Act
then some of the liberty that we value so highly in the field of education begins to fly out the window.
There is another questionable angle to this resolution and it is this. It places those responsible for education in a position where they are obliged to go from door to door among the corporations and in effect ask for hand-outs. I greatly regret the situation of which I learned when not so long ago I met one of the most intelligent heads of one of our most progressive universities returning from New York. What had he been doing in New York? He had been spending a week in New York approaching these United States corporations having large subsidiaries in Canada, and he was appealing to them for funds for his university. He was a man chosen to head the affairs of the university. Yet because of the conditions existing he had been placed in a position where he was a beggar on behalf of the university rather than the able administrator supplying the intelligent leadership which he was able to supply and for which purpose he had been appointed in the first place.
While I am not in opposition to the resolution at this time I think the wiser approach for the good of education is not to take the approach the minister took when he introduced this matter in his budget speech. I think the wiser approach is this. If these corporations are making more than the shareholders must have, if they are making more money than they require, then the money should be collected from them by way of taxation by various levels of government and the government can hand that money over to those institutions of learning thereby assuring the continuing liberty of our schools of learning.
We just have to look south of the 49th parallel to see what can happen. All Canadians interested in the field of education are expressing growing concern at how one institution after another south of the border is beginning to become subject to the huge corporations upon whose generosity they must rely for their continued existence. We do not wish that to happen in our Dominion of Canada. I hope the minister will hold some consultations with responsible educators in Canada-I do not mean only scientists but men really in the field of education-upon the long-range possibilities of some of the implications of the government encouraging corporations to make their donations to schools of higher learning rather than the government taking this money from the corporations and the government remaining in charge of our schools of learning.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
I wish to make a comment or two on this matter, Mr. Chairman. I 
have had something to do with universities, their needs for money and their collection of money from corporations. It seems to me that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam has insisted on bringing into this discussion a measure of suspicion of all kinds of dark doings which are going to be let loose if this exemption is increased in the case of corporations.
That is your interpretation.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I have had some experience in these matters and while there may be cases where corporations try to exercise an influence and perhaps, in rare cases, undue influence, I would also point out that there are a great many corporations who give money and give it gladly and leave it to, we hope, the wise decisions of the university boards as to its use. It seems to me that to cavil at these concessions made to corporations who do not subscribe is utterly unnecessary and that we should give our blessing to this provision.

I wonder whether I might, with great respect, make a suggestion to the minister. I believe we are all agreed that it would be well for the educational and charitable institutions of the country and for the people generally if all corporations could in some manner be induced to take full advantage of the law and to pay to these worthy institutions the full 5 per cent, now 10 per cent, of their earnings. Would the minister consider at the end of each year tabling in this -house a list of those Canadian corporations who have taken full advantage of the law and another list of those who have not done so? I think the country is entitled to know-
How about individuals?

Well, we could include individuals too, if you like, but we are discussing a special law at this moment with respect to corporations. I do not object to individuals being treated in a like manner and I would in fact support such a resolution. However, I believe most individuals do take advantage of this provision, right up to the hilt, and I believe the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Finance will agree that it is unlikely that any individual does not do so. Therefore the hon. member might reflect upon his observation and he may realize that these things could be improved upon.
I	hope the minister will consider the tabling of two such lists concerning corporations operating under federal charters in Canada. We want to know which of those organizations are discharging their responsibilities to the charitable and educational institutions of our country and which are not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, I could not recommend such a course, which would mean not only a departure from but a complete violation of the principle of secrecy as applied to income tax returns.
In principle, I do not think that is the way to bring about the desired result; I think we must depend upon the good judgment of the people, and the element of compulsion is not, in my opinion, a desirable one to be introduced by this house. We might deplore the fact that many corporations do not measure up to what my hon. friend and I regard as their proper social responsibilities, but in time, as the result of education, we trust there will be a better response, to which we hope this present change will contribute.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is there any further discussion on the paragraph or shall we proceed to the fourth paragraph?
Agreed.

Mr. Chairman, I noticed with considerable interest the other day, after this resolution was presented to the house, that a tax commentator in the Financial Post had this to say:
The amendment apparently ignores the effect of the exchequer court decision in the case of Subsidiaries Holding Co. Ltd. v. the Queen in which it was held that a taxpayer may not enforce payment of a refund refused by the department-even if the refusal is not legally justifiable on the merits of the case.
The extension of time will be of no use to taxpayers faced with a departmental refusal to pay.
I see that this refers to the next paragraph, and I will reserve that question for the moment, but on the fourth paragraph I have another question to raise.
Am I right in thinking that the self-employed person is obligated to pay a quarterly amount in respect of tax and, if not, there is a penalty of interest imposed upon him? I read a newspaper statement the other day to the effect that the employed person whose wages are deducted at source is under a considerable disadvantage, and it was pointed out that if a self-employed person had put aside for his own use the amount of tax that would otherwise be deducted monthly he would save, at the end of the year, in the case of a man earning $4,000 per annum, at 3 per cent, interest $5.64 if he was a married man, and $9.85 if he was single man. This would constitute an advantage to that extent over the man whose tax was deducted at source each month and a question, of course, arises with respect to the fact that no interest is allowed on advance payments of income tax. I would like to ask, therefore, if it is true that a selfemployed person does not have to present 57071-3-1354
Income Tax Act
his tax return or pay his tax liability until the April 30 after the year in which the income was earned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He is obliged to make quarterly instalment payments, and I think my hon. friend will find the answer to his question in section 54 of the act.
Could the minister inform the house of the amount paid by the department last year as interest on over-payments of tax, that is to say, for the last fiscal year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Those figures are
not available, Mr. Chairman.

Would the minister explain why they are not available? If the rate was 2 per cent and the government wants to increase it to 3 per cent, there must be a reason for so doing and something must have been paid.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, of course, and the reason is obvious. The government wishes to be a little more generous to the taxpayer to whom the refund is payable, but the fiscal year closed on March 31, which was three and a half months ago, and the figures have not been compiled, so they are simply not available.
Could the minister give the figure for the year ending March 31, 1957, which was two years ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The department does not segregate those figures.

Mr. Chairman, there must be a reason for this. The minister has just stated that the government wants to be more generous to the taxpayer and 1 think this committee has a right to know how much money was paid during the last fiscal year for which the figures are available. We should be told what difference it would make to the treasury and how much more money would be involved. Are we being asked to vote blindly on a flat statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My friend may not approve of the fact but, nevertheless, the figures are not available. No statistical records have been taken of the precise amount paid by way of interest on refunds under the existing law.
Is this not a poor way to deal with these matters, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Might I remind my hon. friend that if the former government had seen fit to amend the law so as to provide for such records we would have those figures today. We have, however, only

Income Tax Act
been in office for a year and we cannot be responsible for failures under the law before that time.
Every time the minister seems to be in a jam he goes back over the last -22 years.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: We are only going back to last year.
If there was anything wrong during the administration of the past 22 years why do you not try to correct it today. I think we have the right to know.
We are correcting things; they cannot all be done in one year. Give us time.

We have a right to know. I hear the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot squeaking away as always. We hear all the time about giving the baby Castoria if he cries; we hear it on the radio, we read it in the newspapers and so on. If he waits a little while I will give him some Castoria.
What I want to know at the present time is whether or not it is the intention of the minister to try to change this situation so that we may get these figures with respect to what the government is paying back in interest to those who have paid their taxes in advance or overpaid their taxes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Only those who are entitled to a refund will receive any interest in these cases, and then subject to determined conditions. This is not the case of the man who has paid in advance but of the man who is entitled to a refund, and it is the view of the government that when a man has paid more than he was legitimately obliged to pay, the 2 per cent interest on the refund to which he was entitled and which has prevailed for many years is inadequate, and that that rate of interest should be increased in favour of the taxpayer from 2 per cent to 3 per cent.
I do not lay down the rules for statistical compilation of the government or of the former government; it was not the practice under the former government to take off a statistical record, segregating what the
2	per cent rate involved in cost to the treasury. So while the hon. member may regret that the figure is not available I can only inform him that the figure is not available and that the present government is not responsible for the fact that it is not available.
The purpose of this clause is to increase in favour of the taxpayer from 2 per cent to
3	per cent the interest to which he is entitled on a refund under conditions prescribed for the purpose. And the interest is calculated

from the latest of three dates; first, the date when the overpayment arises; second, the date on or before which the return was required to be filed; and third, the date when the return was actually filed; and the interest runs to the day on which the overpayment of the tax is refunded.

The minister or his department must have made some estimate of what it would mean to the treasury to increase this interest rate from 2 per cent to 3 per cent. It must mean that a certain sum of money would not be available to the treasury. There must be an estimate somewhere.
Has the minister not got any idea? Is it $50 or $500?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are many occasions on which a precise estimate of cost to the treasury with respect to a particular change in the tax law cannot be arrived at, and this is a case in which there has been no precise estimate, and in which no attempt has been made to arrive at a precise estimate. It is a measure which is put forward because it is considered to offer more justice to the taxpayer.
May I ask if this rise in the interest rate is an indication of an expected rise in the interest rate generally?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. It will not have escaped the attention of the hon. member that it remains for a government which has had the satisfaction of seeing interest rates brought down substantially since it came to office to propose this increase in the interest rate on refunds due to the taxpayer.

Is it the intention of the minister to fix a date after which it will assume responsibility for his own administration? The Minister of Finance refers to what the former government did. Is he going to set an ultimate date after which he will assume his own responsibility?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that is a subject for a private chat between the hon. gentleman and myself.

The minister tells us that he has no estimate of what this increase will cost the treasury. Did he not ask his officers what this additional one per cent would mean? If the minister never got around to this, why did he not make the figure 4 per cent, or why did he not increase the rate to 5 per cent? It would not mean anything, because there is nothing to show the cost.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think if we were to increase it to that extent even the hon.

member would be overpaying his tax in order to obtain a high rate of interest on his return.
What is the rate charged to those who are late in paying.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I thought the
hon. member was well aware of that. It is well known. It is 6 per cent.
Why not make it 6 per cent for refund?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Because the 6 per cent is in the nature of a penalty.

The government should be
penalized because sometimes, when they overpay, it is because the amount has been poorly calculated in the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am deeply impressed by the hon. member's keen desire to see the present government penalized, but he was here for quite a few years and he never suggested that the previous government should be penalized in this way.
There is something the minister will have to learn. From now on we are dealing with the future and not with the past.
Would the minister not hold Sir John A. Macdonald responsible?

Mr. Chairman, I think there is a close relationship between overpayment as described in this paragraph and a subject in which the minister himself has always taken an interest, and that is overdeduction. I am not criticizing the administration, but I wonder if it would not be appropriate at this time for some statistics to be given, if they are available, to indicate the extent to which it is proving necessary to make refunds to people who have their taxes deducted at source. We might have some figures as to the amount of money so refunded in recent years and the number of taxpayers entitled to refunds each year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I suggest that is a proper question to ask the Minister of National Revenue when his estimates are before the committee of supply?

Before we pass on from the question which has been brought up by hon. members to my right I think it would be a good thing if the minister would indicate if this government intends to change the policy which has been in effect for a number of years so that in future we may have an accounting of how much is involved, because it seems to me there should be an accounting
Income Tax Act
figure somewhere to show what it represents. It seems to me it is time there was a change in the way this is done.

I am concerned about who it is who receives this interest rate. I have never heard of individuals receiving interest out of the government. Must the money lie on deposit, for years before a taxpayer is eligible to be paid any interest? I believe there are hundreds of thousands of Canadians who are eligible for some manner of refund at the end of the tax year. Is this 2 per cent regularly added to the refund or must there be a certain minimum amount? Under what conditions is any interest paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The fact that the hon. member has not heard of many cases is I think a tribute to the efforts of the Department of National Revenue to make these refunds before April 30, and I think it is not amiss to pay tribute to my colleague the Minister of National Revenue for the efforts which are being made in this respect.
In other words, if I understand the minister aright, there is no interest payable on money before April 30. It is only payable on money left after that date.
I hope the Minister of National Revenue will not say it should have been asked on the resolution on income tax.
Would the minister care to explain the intention of paragraph 5.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I thought paragraph 5 was obvious.
I think it should be on the record, that is all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is very obvious at the present time that any application on the part of a taxpayer for a refund in respect of overpayment must be made within two years from the end of the taxation year in question. Cases have arisen where the taxpayer, following the expiration of the two-year period, has found some mistake. It may be that he made a mistake in his own return or, for some reason or other, he considers he has overpaid and wishes to apply for a refund. Under the present law the only way to deal with such a case is for the governor in council to permit an ex-gratia payment to be made, and that is not the way in which these cases should be handled. Therefore it is proposed that the period be now extended from two to four years within which a taxpayer may apply for a refund.

Does the minister have any figure to show what it would cost the treasury to extend it for an additional two years?

Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is quite obvious, Mr. Chairman, that Solomon himself could not give a figure on that because these are cases that are unknown at the present time. There may be cases that will arise where, after the two-year period, the taxpayer will discover he has a claim to a refund and will make it, but those cases are not known at the present time.
Does the minister not know that Solomon was a pretty good accountant himself? He was able to count up to 1,000, at least.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I always understood that Solomon lost count after 600.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: He just lost interest after 600.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall we proceed to a discussion of paragraph No. 6?

Mr. Chairman, I see in this paragraph that a gift to a spouse of real property can qualify for exemption from payment of gift tax. In the province of Quebec we have a marriage contract which has to be signed before the marriage. Would that be included in that? In other provinces you can sign a marriage contract or give a gift after the marriage but in the province of Quebec marriage contracts have to be signed before the marriage takes place. I would like to have some clarification of that point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The nub of the
problem would be the effective date, not of the contract but of the gift. This provides for a gift between spouses.
But it is a gift by contract. If a man were to give a gift of $10,000 in real property to his wife before the marriage will that be included?

His wife? Before the
marriage?
His wife-to-be. Assume they are to be married in two days.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is assuming there will be no slip twixt the cup and the lip; but I do not know that the law in all those cases can assume that the intended marriage is going to be carried out. The resolution contemplates a gift from one spouse to another.

Paragraph 6 is a good example of how the tax drafters have considered only English common law and not Quebec civil law. In the province of Quebec the question of gifts between husbands and wives is regulated, as hon. members know, fey the civil code. In order to give a gift to your, wife you must specify it in the marriage contract which, as was pointed out by my

friend the hon. member for Hull, has to be signed before the marriage. If the minister is prepared to give an exemption of $10,000 to people living in English-speaking provinces, why would he not consider giving an exemption of $10,000 on gifts made between husbands and wives and allow the province of Quebec to participate in this general provision because transfers of property between husband and wife-I was going to say are not well known, but in fact they are not even permitted in Quebec as I understand they are in English-speaking provinces?
While I am on my feet, I have a few questions to ask with regard to paragraph six. I note that the paragraph refers to gifts of real property. Does this apply to a gift of cash to buy real property, cash per se and cash to forgive indebtedness arising from the previous purchase of real property?
I also ask this question. If you claim an exemption of $10,000 once on account of a gift of a house between husband and wife, can you also claim a second exemption for the gift of a farm to your son?
Another question arises. Let us assume that I claim only $5,000 of my $10,000 exemption. Can I come later and claim the balance of $5,000? Can I in effect make two gifts up to the extent of $10,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Taking my hon. friend's points seriatim, in the first place if it is permissible under the laws of Quebec, the competent draftsman my hon. friend is would seek to provide that the gift which is ante-nuptial in effect, would take effect on the marriage. In that case if the gift were one of real property it would obviously come within the scope of the present resolution.
I believe the next question my friend asked was whether cash could be substituted for a gift of real estate and the answer is no. The law at the present time permits a gift of $4,000 per annum, but the purpose of this provision is to create more security in the Canadian home for the spouse and, of course, particularly for the wife. That is the whole purpose of the clause.
My hon. friend asked about the possibility of two gifts, a gift to the spouse and then, if the property should happen to be a farm property, a gift to the son. The answer is that there is one gift permitted and only one of $10,000 in value. My hon. friend realizes that this is in addition, of course, to the present permissible gift of $4,000 per annum.

During the course of the afternoon I referred to a subject and perhaps I gave the minister a bit of a running start because it is dealt with in this paragraph. In the very best of faith there is an

oversight in this paragraph in so far as the citizens of the province of Quebec are concerned. Perhaps I discussed this subject this afternoon under a heading which may have made me slightly out of order and ' I would like to repeat my remarks now and ask the minister to examine the question.
Husbands and wives in Quebec who have no ante-nuptial contracts are considered to be common as to property. That is the law of the province. In fact, Quebec is the only province in the whole of Canada with that peculiarity in its law. Consequently a husband in that province who is common as to property with his wife-I am not concerned about the separation as to property at the moment-is prevented under this paragraph from taking advantage of giving a gift to his wife as contemplated by this clause.
I can visualize the following situation. A husband who is common as to property in Quebec might wish to give or pass to his wife $10,000 ownership in the home which they occupy, and I use that figure because that is the restriction under this paragraph. Property cannot be conveyed in Quebec, as it can in other provinces, unless it is done by notarial deed. The husband and wife must go to a notary to have such a deed drawn up. A notary who is ethical and who knows his law will promptly say to him, "Under article 1265 of the civil code of the province of Quebec you cannot make a gift to your wife."
Assuming a notary were to draw up such a deed and the husband died later, the succession duty assessors who are very able and knowledgeable gentlemen, in assessing the estate must find that the gift which the husband gave to his wife is completely void and the $10,000 would revert to the estate.
I am to give an example. A husband who is worth $100,000 ostensibly gives his wife under this section a gift of a $10,000 interest in the home. When he dies the value of his estate should then be $90,000 because he has parted with $10,000 by a legal gift to his wife under this section. Assuming there are no children, she is entitled to an exemption of $60,000 leaving a taxable estate of $30,000. But in assessing the estate the inspectors will find the flaw in this gift. It is a gift that is void. It is not even voidable. It is void ab initio. Consequently there is an estate of $40,000 on which succession duties .must be paid.
As I said this afternoon, I think that some provision should be made to allow husbands or wives in the province of Quebec who are common as to property to' benefit from this form of gift. I have discussed the matter with lawyers who are perhaps more familiar
Income Tax Act
with the civil law than I am and they have confirmed the suspicion that this clause will not afford the same benefit and have the same force and effect in the province of Quebec as elsewhere. Therefore I suggest to the minister that perhaps between now and the bringing down of the bill he might give this matter very careful consideration. Perhaps some means can be devised to allow the province of Quebec to enjoy the fullest advantages of this section in the same way as the other provinces of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Even according
to my hon. friend's contention, it is not this section which denies the benefit to the Quebec spouse. According to his argument it is the law of Quebec-
Correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-so he should
not say it is this provision which denies benefit to the Quebec spouse. I want to point out to him that the spouse in Quebec, as between whom and his spouse there is community of property, does not need this clause. There is community of property between them and they therefore share ownership of the family home. There is a situation which does not exist in the other provinces, and surely my hon. friend is not going to deny the opportunity, so far as tax legislation can do it, to extend the benefit of community of property to spouses in the other provinces in respect of the family home.

The fact does remain though that it is intended under this section to allow a husband to make a gift to his wife free of gift tax. That can happen without any difficulty in any of the other provinces of Canada. The husband can make a gift to his wife free of gift tax. Under the laws of the province of Quebec this is not possible under this section.
What we are saying in effect is that the gift tax provisions should allow the husband to pay $10,000 to his wife under his marriage contract free of gift tax. That is what we want.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I did not catch
that.
We are asking that the law should be amended to allow a husband who has a marriage contract in the province of Quebec to pay $10,000 to his wife free of gift tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This provision is not intended to be a duplication of the present provision with regard to the $4,000 per annum which a husband may give to his Wife. That

Income Tax Act
stands. This is intended to create security for the wife in the ownership of the family home. It is related directly to the family home and that is the purpose of it. It does not relate to cash gifts at all. It permits a gift of an interest in the home.

In the province of Quebec husbands are not allowed to give gifts to wives or wives to husbands. How will we do it? They can do it up to 48 hours before they sign the marriage contract. Would they be exempted from gift tax? If not, I think it is a case of discrimination against the laws of the province of Quebec which are not the same as in the rest of Canada. We still have the Napoleon code.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This provision, which has much to commend it, is available to anybody in Canada once parliament enacts it. If it is my hon. friend's opinion that the law of Quebec prevents some spouses there from deriving benefit from this provision, I think in all fairness that should not be pleaded as a reason for denying this benefit to spouses in other provinces, particularly when it is a fact that those spouses in Quebec as between whom community of property exists already have similar benefits.

Would it not be possible to
amend clause 6 to provide that gifts given under the marriage contract which is signed a few hours or a day before the marriage will be considered as gifts given to a spouse and be exempt from gift tax? That is what we want. We do not want to stop others from benefiting but we want those in the province of Quebec to be able to have this benefit.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
The hon. member is speaking about the province of Quebec where under certain circumstances they have community of property. From what I have seen in my limited practice, and I am sure others in English-speaking provinces have seen it too, a husband will deed a property to his wife as joint tenant. Perhaps they build a home when the husband retires and they create a joint tenancy. Then the husband dies and in the course of events it is suddenly found that there is a gift tax because the property is owned by the husband and the wife had not put any money into it. Time and time again complications have arisen because of the gift tax and gift tax assessments. It is to avoid cases such as that that this section is designed. It refers to the home of the husband and wife.
I think you will all agree that when they start out early in life the husband buys a home. That is all right. But later on they retire and he may build or buy another home. The probabilities of life expectancy being what they are, the chances are that he will
pass on before his wife and the husband may create a joint tenancy. But then complications may arise because of the gift tax. This section is designed largely, so far as husbands and wives are concerned, to overcome that difficulty and that difficulty only. There is also, of course, the feature of encouraging a father to turn over his farm property to his son and thus avoid payment of gift tax as has happened so often in the past. It is remedial legislation.

I do not doubt at all the
lofty and desirable intentions of this section of the law but I am a little apprehensive whether or not it delivers that which it seems to deliver so far as husbands and wives in the province of Quebec are concerned. If it does and if the minister is satisfied that it does then we want him to convince us. I appreciate the lofty intentions which motivated the section. I agree with it and accept it but, as I said, I am very doubtful whether or not, in so far as the province of Quebec is concerned, it will be as effective, useful and helpful as the minister has just said it will be in other provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Give us a chance to put it to work and let us see then whether my friend's misgivings or our hopes are justified.

Perhaps the minister could get a legal opinion in the course of the next few days in order to assure the house that the section will deliver that which he thinks it will deliver. Perhaps he could get a legal opinion from the Department of Justice or the Minister of Justice. We would like to have a legal opinion.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Are we finished with paragraph 6?

No. I call it ten o'clock.
Progress reported.
